## Why This Is Asked

This question tests practical CKAD skills: dynamic configuration via ConfigMaps, per-namespace isolation, InitContainers, health checks, logging, and network policy considerations.

## Key Concepts

- **Namespace-scoped ConfigMaps**: Enable dynamic feature flags without pod restarts
- **InitContainers**: Provide bootstrap tooling (curl) before the main container starts
- **Conditional sidecars**: Driven by ConfigMap values to enable canary deployments
- **Readiness and liveness probes**: Ensure controller and application health
- **PVC-backed logs**: Provide persistent storage for debugging and audit trails
- **NetworkPolicies**: Enforce zero-trust networking by restricting egress to known endpoints

## Trade-offs

| Aspect | Consideration |
|--------|----------------|
| **Polling Interval** | Frequent polls increase API load; infrequent polls delay flag propagation |
| **ConfigMap Updates** | Applications must watch or periodically read the ConfigMap to detect changes |
| **Sidecar Overhead** | Running a sidecar even when disabled consumes resources; consider whether the main container can react to flag changes directly |
| **Egress Restriction** | Locking down NetworkPolicy requires knowing all upstream dependencies upfront |
| **Log Persistence** | PVCs add operational complexity and cost; consider external logging solutions for production |

## Minimal YAML Skeleton

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: feature-flags
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: feature-flags
  namespace: feature-flags
data:
  flags.json: '{}'
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: logs-pvc
  namespace: feature-flags
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: flag-poller
  namespace: feature-flags
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: flag-poller
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: flag-poller
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-curl
          image: curlimages/curl:latest
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'cp /usr/bin/curl /tools/curl']
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /tools
      containers:
        - name: poller
          image: your-poller-image:latest
          command: ['/bin/sh', '-c', 'while true; do curl -s $FLAGS_API > /config/flags.json; sleep 60; done']
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
        - name: sidecar
          image: your-sidecar-image:latest
          env:
            - name: FEATURE_ENABLED
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: feature-flags
                  key: enabled
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: feature-flags
        - name: tools
          emptyDir: {}
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-pvc
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: flags-egress-policy
  namespace: feature-flags
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: flag-poller
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: flags-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
```

This design balances flexibility with operational simplicity, making it well-suited for Kubernetes feature management in multi-tenant environments.

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to compose a small, repeatable namespace-scoped app using InitContainers, volumes, and secret/config data. It also checks understanding of namespace governance via ResourceQuota, LimitRange, and NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts

- InitContainer run-before-main-container ensures content is prepared at startup
- EmptyDir volumes for ephemeral assets; ConfigMap/Secret mounted as files
- ResourceQuota and LimitRange to cap per-namespace usage
- Namespace NetworkPolicy to restrict egress to allowed endpoints
- Minimal YAML skeletons and clear trade-offs

## Code Example

```yaml
# ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: content-config
data:
  CONTENT_URL: "https://content-api.local/assets"
```

```yaml
# Secret (base64-encoded token)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: content-secret
type: Opaque
data:
  API_TOKEN: <base64-token>
```

```yaml
# Deployment skeleton (2 replicas) with InitContainer and volumes
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: static-content-host
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: fetch-assets
          image: curlimages/curl:7.83.1
          command: ["sh", "-c", "CONTENT_URL=$(cat /config/CONTENT_URL); TOKEN=$(cat /secret/API_TOKEN); curl -sS -H 'Authorization: Bearer '$TOKEN $CONTENT_URL -o /assets/index.html"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: assets
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
            - name: secret
              mountPath: /secret
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          volumeMounts:
            - name: assets
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
      volumes:
        - name: assets
          emptyDir: {}
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: content-config
        - name: secret
          secret:
            secretName: content-secret
```

```yaml
# Service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: static-content-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: static-content-host
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
      protocol: TCP
  type: ClusterIP
```

```yaml
# ResourceQuota (namespace-wide)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: ns-quota
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "10"
```

```yaml
# LimitRange (default limits)
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: ns-limits
spec:
  limits:
    - max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 2Gi
      min:
        cpu: "100m"
        memory: 128Mi
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 512Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      type: Container
```

```yaml
# NetworkPolicy (egress only to content API)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-egress-to-content-api
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 203.0.113.0/24
```

- What are the trade-offs of using InitContainer vs a sidecar for content updates?

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical CKAD skills, including permissioning, automation, and Kubernetes-native policy enforcement using a CronJob with ConfigMap-driven behavior.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped CronJob for periodic enforcement
- ConfigMap-driven policy configuration (imageRepo, imageTag)
- kubectl patch or server-side apply for image updates
- PVC-based logging and HTTP POST for audit trails
- InitContainer for tooling installation (curl, jq)
- Namespace NetworkPolicy scoping for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: image-tag-enforcer
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: busybox
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl jq"]
          containers:
          - name: enforcer
            image: curlimages/curl:latest
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
            args:
            - |
              # Read policy from ConfigMap
              # Get all Deployments in namespace
              # Compare images against policy
              # Patch mismatched Deployments
              # Write heartbeat log to /logs
              # POST summary to policy-portal
            volumeMounts:
            - name: log-volume
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/ready"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/alive"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: log-volume
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: enforcer-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: policy-portal
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
```

## Trade-offs
- **Frequency**: Running every 5 minutes balances responsiveness vs. resource usage; longer intervals reduce API load but delay remediation
- **PVC vs. Sidecar**: Using a PVC is simpler but requires storage provisioning; a sidecar could stream logs directly
- **Patch vs. Reconcile Controller**: A declarative controller would be more robust but requires custom operator development; CronJob is quicker to implement but imperative
- **InitContainer**: Pre-installing tools increases pod startup time; consider using a custom image with tools baked in instead
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricting egress improves security but may break legitimate communication; ensure all required endpoints are explicitly allowed
- **Idempotency**: Multiple enforcers running simultaneously could cause conflicts; consider adding a lock mechanism or using `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid`

- PVC-backed persistent logs and InitContainers for tooling
- NetworkPolicy for egress control to restrict traffic to the collector
- Health checks (readiness/liveness probes) for reliability

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: audit-baseline
  namespace: example
data:
  baseline.json: |
    {"pods": [], "services": []}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: audit-auth
  namespace: example
type: Opaque
stringData:
  token: " collector-auth-token"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: audit-logs
  namespace: example
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: audit-agent
  namespace: example
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: audit-agent
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: audit-agent
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl jq && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tools
          mountPath: /tools
      containers:
      - name: auditor
        image: your-audit-image:latest
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do audit.sh; sleep 60; done"]
        env:
        - name: COLLECTOR_URL
          value: "http://collector.audit-system.svc.cluster.local:8080"
        - name: AUTH_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: audit-auth
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        - name: tools
          mountPath: /tools
        - name: baseline
          mountPath: /baseline
          readOnly: true
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: audit-logs
      - name: tools
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: baseline
        configMap:
          name: audit-baseline
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: audit-egress-restrict
  namespace: example
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: audit-agent
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: audit-system
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: collector
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
```

## Trade-offs
- **Pros**: Namespace isolation ensures audit agents don't interfere; NetworkPolicy provides security; PVC enables log persistence for compliance
- **Cons**: Each namespace requires separate Deployment (use Operator/Controller to automate); InitContainer adds startup latency; per-namespace RBAC management overhead increases with cluster size

## Why This Is Asked

  name: compliance-guard
  namespace: your-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: compliance-guard
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: compliance-guard
    spec:
      initContainers:

## Why This Matters
This question validates practical Kubernetes skills: namespace-level resource enforcement, working with defaults, and ensuring application reliability through probes and update strategies.

## Key Concepts
- **LimitRange**: Applies default requests/limits to containers without explicit resources. The `defaultRequest` sets what gets requested if not specified; `default` sets the limit.
- **ResourceQuota**: Hard caps preventing namespace resource exhaustion. Tracks usage against hard limits.
- **readinessProbe**: Ensures traffic reaches only ready pods. Uses `/health` HTTP endpoint on port 8080.
- **RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 0**: Ensures zero-downtime updates by keeping all old pods running until new ones are ready.

## Verification Under Load
Apply quota/limits first, then patch the deployment. Verify pods receive defaults via `kubectl get pod -o jsonpath`. Under load, confirm quota usage updates and readiness probes correctly gate traffic. The rolling update strategy ensures zero downtime during config changes.

## Rollback
Use `kubectl rollout undo` to revert to previous revision. With `maxUnavailable: 0`, rollback is also zero-downtime. Check revision history with `kubectl rollout history`.

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical CKAD skills including per-namespace configuration management, InitContainer usage, sidecar patterns, secure secret handling, and network policy implementation.

## Key Concepts
- Per-namespace deployments with shared persistent volumes
- InitContainer for runtime dependency installation
- Inotify-based file change detection and yamllint validation
- In-service reload capabilities (nginx -s reload)
- ConfigMap and Secret integration patterns
- TLS sidecar implementation for secure communications
- Namespace-level NetworkPolicy for egress restrictions

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton of the Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-watcher
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: config-watcher
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: config-watcher
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'apk add --no-cache inotify-tools yamllint']
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-pvc
          mountPath: /config/dynamic
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
      - name: config-watcher
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'while inotifywait -e modify /config/dynamic/*.yaml; do yamllint /config/dynamic/*.yaml && nginx -s reload; done']
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-pvc
          mountPath: /config/dynamic
        env:
        - name: STATUS_URL
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: status-secret
              key: url
      - name: tls-sidecar
        image: envoyproxy/envoy:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8443
      volumes:
      - name: config-pvc
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: config-pvc
      - name: nginx-defaults
        configMap:
          name: nginx-defaults
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: config-pvc
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nginx-defaults
  namespace: target-namespace
data:
  nginx.conf: |
    # Default Nginx configuration
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: status-secret
  namespace: target-namespace
type: Opaque
data:
  url: aHR0cDovL3N0YXR1cy5sb2NhbC9hcGkvdjEvcmVsb2Fk
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: config-watcher-netpol
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: config-watcher
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: internal-services
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
```

## Trade-offs
- **Inotify vs polling**: Inotify is more efficient but requires file system support
- **Sidecar overhead**: TLS sidecar adds complexity and resource usage
- **Single namespace scope**: Limited to namespace-level isolation vs cluster-wide
- **PVC dependency**: Requires storage management and backup strategies
- **Container sharing**: Process communication within pod vs separate services
